The Value Chain

A study guide to the reading: what the framework is, how to run it, and what it reveals about profit. Click anything that looks interactive.

Porter's value chain

Michael Porter's 1985 idea breaks a firm into the activities it performs. Competitive advantage lives in those activities, not in the firm as a whole, because a firm has no costs. Activities do. Porter sorted them into nine generic boxes.

The chain (tap a box)

Blue-green boxes are primary activities that touch the product on its way to the buyer. Gold boxes are support activities that run across all of them.
Inbound logistics
Operations
Outbound logistics
Marketing and sales
Service
Firm infrastructure
Human resources
Technology development
Procurement
Profit margin: what is left when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the total cost of everything to the left

Two things people miss

1. The boxes are a starting point. Split an activity when its parts have different economics. "Operations" at an airline is not one activity: gate turnaround and engine overhaul share almost nothing.

2. The advantage often sits between the boxes. Porter calls these linkages: the cost of one activity depends on how another is done. More inbound inspection means less rework. More inventory means less expediting.

Why linkages make chains hard to copy

A rival can see any single activity: store layouts, shelf prices, job postings, patents. What it cannot easily see is which activity is subsidizing which.

Amazon's 2023 network redesign is the reading's example. No single activity got cheaper. The relationships among them changed, and cost per unit fell for the first time since 2018.

How to run a value chain analysis

The framework only describes. The analysis is five steps. Each step has a predictable way to fail when you skip its questions. Open each one.

Little Caesars is the only one of the four big pizza chains below the industry average. Datassential calls it the value leader. It wins on price perception and loses on satisfaction, which is what a low-price, low-volume position looks like from outside.

The key distinction. A value chain analysis tells you where the cost went out. It does not tell you who kept it. In this case, the savings were partly captured by the franchisor through a mandatory supply relationship and the highest fee load in the category.

Own one link

The opposite of Little Caesars is to take one activity and perform it so far beyond anyone else that the rest of the industry comes to you. Five examples, one per activity.

Inbound logistics

ASML: lithography

The only maker of EUV lithography systems, with an estimated 94 percent share of all lithography (JPMorgan estimate). 2025 sales of €32.7 billion, 52.8 percent gross margin, 34.6 percent operating margin, €38.8 billion backlog.

The mechanism: ASML is a systems integrator coordinating about 5,100 suppliers. In 2016 it bought 24.9 percent of Carl Zeiss SMT, the only optics house that can make EUV mirrors. A rival would have to rebuild a supplier network built over three decades.

Operations

TSMC: fabrication capacity

Owns no product designs. Took 72.5 percent of global foundry revenue in Q2 2026 (a record), with a 67.7 percent gross margin and 60.3 percent operating margin. Samsung had 5.9 percent.

The mechanism: A promise, not a technology. TSMC never competes with its customers. That let Nvidia, Apple, AMD and Qualcomm shed their fabs, which concentrated demand, which funds the node lead.

Operations (supplier)

YKK: zippers

About 40 percent of the world's zippers, more than 10 billion units in the year to March 2025. It smelts its own brass, makes its own alloys, dyes its tape, and builds its own fastening machinery.

The mechanism: It leases machines into customers' factories, so its fixed assets sit on the garment maker's floor. The zipper is about 1 percent of a garment's cost, yet its logo is often the only one on the product.

Caveat: YKK is private and publishes no margins. The reading says so out loud.

Outbound logistics

Amazon: parcels

In calendar 2025 it delivered 6.7 billion US parcels, passing USPS and becoming the largest carrier. In May 2026 it began selling the capability through Amazon Supply Chain Services.

The mechanism: An internal cost center, optimized until it became an advantage, then sold to the incumbents' own customers. FedEx and UPS shares each fell about 10 percent on the news.

Service

The Ritz-Carlton

Any employee may spend up to $2,000 on the spot to fix a guest problem. Revenue per available room beat the industry by more than 300 percent. Pre-tax ROI nearly doubled from 5.3 to 9.8 percent (1995 to 1998). First-year staff trained 250 to 310 hours. Turnover fell nine straight years.

Source is a 1999 Baldrige profile. Treat the figures as historical, not current.

Profit pools: where the money sits

If activities have different economics, the money piles up in some parts of any chain. A value chain map comes from your own ledger and shows where costs are. A profit pool map comes from industry filings and shows where everyone's profits are. The first is an efficiency tool. The second asks whether you stand in the right part of the chain at all.

A car dealership, from public filings (AutoNation, 2025)

Total: $27.6 billion of sales and $4.9 billion of gross profit. Finance and insurance is derived here: it is the combined 22.8 percent (revenue) and 77.2 percent (gross profit) minus parts and service. Calculated from the disclosed dollar figures.

Parts, service, finance and insurance are 22.8 percent of sales and 77.2 percent of gross profit. New vehicles are 48.9 percent of revenue and only 13.4 percent of gross profit.

Check yourself

Tap a question to reveal the answer. Then read the cheat sheet.

1. What does Porter say a firm actually has?
No costs. Activities have costs. A firm wins or loses in each activity separately.
2. Name the two kinds of linkage the reading uses as an example.
Inbound inspection reduces rework. Holding inventory reduces expediting. Also: designing a part to snap instead of bolt shortens assembly.
3. Why does Little Caesars' low price only work with high throughput per labor hour?
Made-ahead production delivers the throughput. Without it, a low price cannot cover labor. Remove any one of narrow menu, made-ahead production, or low price and the other two stop making sense.
4. Why is Little Caesars' volume a fragility rather than a strength?
It pairs low cost with low throughput, unlike Walmart. Fixed chain costs (distribution, national advertising, brand) are spread over fewer dollars.
5. What is a profit pool, and how does it differ from a value chain map?
A profit pool is the total profit earned at every point along an industry's chain. The value chain map uses your own ledger to show costs. The profit pool uses industry filings to show where everyone's profits sit. The first is an efficiency instrument; the second is a positioning instrument.
6. Why does the reading say the pattern of profit differs from revenue?
Profit concentrates in different places than revenue. In a car dealership, parts, service, finance and insurance are 22.8 percent of sales but 77.2 percent of gross profit.
7. What did Amazon's 2023 network redesign change, and what did it not change?
It regionalized the US into eight largely self-sufficient regions. No single activity got cheaper. The relationships among them changed, and cost per unit fell.
8. What is the "key distinction" the reading ends on?
A value chain analysis shows where the cost went out. It does not show who kept it. Ask both questions.

Draw your own chain

Type in your activities (one per box). Split the ones with different economics. Then ask the question the reading ends on.

    If you could defend only one of these to the last dollar, which would it be, and is it the one you are funding?

    One-card cheat sheet

    1. Value chain: a firm is a set of activities, each with a cost. Advantage lives in the activities and the links between them.
    2. Run it in five steps: split by economics, attach cost and assets, find cost drivers (ten of them), work the linkages, decide make vs. buy.
    3. Linkages: the hard-to-copy part. Competitors can see activities but not which ones subsidize which.
    4. Delete an activity is the most reliable cost cut, because matching a rival's performance invites a response.
    5. Own one link: be so good at one activity that the industry comes to you (ASML, TSMC, YKK, Amazon).
    6. Profit pool: map where industry profit sits, using filings. Revenue and profit concentrate in different places.
    7. Two questions: where did the cost go out, and who kept it?

    Source notes. This guide summarizes one reading. Figures are as the reading reports them, mid-September 2026. Where the reading marks a figure as an estimate (Little Caesars volume, the lithography share, the current price, the coffee breakdown), this guide keeps that label.

    • Porter, Competitive Advantage (1985), Ch. 2 and 3.
    • Gadiesh and Gilbert, "Profit Pools" and "How to Map Your Industry's Profit Pool," HBR 1998.
    • AutoNation FY2025 results; Delta FY2025; Booking Holdings FY2025; ASML FY2025; TSMC Q2 2026 (via TrendForce).

The big idea

A five-dollar pizza sat in a warming rack in Michigan from 2004 until January 2022. The easy explanation is cheap cheese. The reading says that is wrong: the price came from a chain of about a dozen activities, each designed to cost less than the same activity at Domino's or Pizza Hut, and one of them (the delivery driver) was simply deleted.

The four takeaways

  1. Firms do not have costs; activities do. Advantage is won or lost activity by activity.
  2. The advantage often sits between the boxes (linkages), which is why chains are hard to copy.
  3. A value chain shows where cost went out, not who kept the savings. Little Caesars' savings were partly captured by the franchisor. Ask both questions.
  4. Profit pools: profit is often concentrated in a very different part of the chain than revenue. Value chain = efficiency tool (your ledger). Profit pool = positioning tool (industry filings).
The closing challenge: draw your chain, split until boxes have different economics, put a cost and an asset on each, then ask: if you could defend only one activity to the last dollar, which is it, and is it the one you are funding?

Porter's chain (1985)

Michael Porter's radical move: stop treating advantage as a property of "well run" firms. A firm is a bundle of discrete activities. Click any box to see what it means and what Little Caesars does there.

Click a box.

Two things routinely missed

1. The boxes are a starting point. Split an activity when its parts have different economics. "Operations" at an airline is not one thing: gate turnaround and engine overhaul have almost nothing in common. If every activity in your chain has the same cost driver, you have not cut finely enough.
2. Advantage may live between the boxes (linkages). A linkage exists when one activity's cost depends on how another is performed. Examples: spend more on inbound inspection, spend less on rework. Hold more inventory, spend less on expediting. Design a snap-fit part, shorten assembly.

How to run a value chain analysis

The framework is descriptive; the analysis is not. Open each step for the question that keeps it honest.

Porter's ten cost drivers

Click to mark the ones you think drive cost in a pretend activity of your own. The point: go through all ten, not just scale.

Test of step 2: "If we had to sell this activity as a standalone business tomorrow, what would its income statement look like?" An activity that is cheap to run but eats working capital is not cheap.

Little Caesars: cost built activity by activity

Key insight: the biggest saving is what LC does not perform at all: no order-taking before making pizza, no drivers, no counter at the Portal. Deleting an activity is the most reliable cost reduction because a rival cannot answer by simply doing it cheaper.

The twist: the story usually told is incomplete

The reading argues LC pairs low cost with low throughput, unlike Walmart (low cost with enormous volume). Fixed costs get spread over fewer dollars.

Average sales per restaurant (QSR, FY2025)

LC is about 69% of Domino's volume, stable for two years. LC figure is a QSR estimate.

Franchisee fee load (royalty + marketing)

Debunked claim: "LC spends less on advertising because the price does the selling." The one mandatory, disclosed comparable says otherwise. Marketing can rise to 7%.

Initial investment floor

Over 4x Domino's, driven by a mandatory pre-opening Blue Line equipment and inventory buy of $250,500 to $369,500. Source caveat: LC's own site says $376,500; the FDD abstracts say $446,500. Unresolved.

Governance contrast: same vertical integration, opposite rules
Domino's
22 US supply chain centers. Franchisees are not required to buy. Those who buy everything get 50% of the supply chain's pre-tax profit. Must win business yearly.
Little Caesars
Blue Line is mandatory (franchisees bought $1.64B in FY2021). No profit share disclosed. Does not have to win it.

The price advantage has narrowed

Hot-N-Ready price: $5 (2004 to Jan 2022), $5.55 (Jan 2022, with 33% more pepperoni), about $6.79 per third-party trackers now. Domino's has repeatedly run a $9.99 "Best Deal Ever". In July 2025 LC launched its first-ever value menu at $9.99, online only. The reading's read: it was following, not setting, and online-only moves the offer away from the walk-in, no-wait, no-decision mechanic the chain was built for.

Satisfaction (ACSI 2026)

LC wins on price perception (Datassential's value leader), loses on satisfaction. "What a low-price, low-volume position looks like from the outside." Yet net US units still grew by 93 in 2025 while the category shrank.

Verdict: A value chain tells you where cost went out. It does not tell you who kept it. Ask both.

Own one link

The opposite of LC's strategy: take one activity and be so far beyond everyone that the industry has to come to you. Tap a card to flip it for the mechanism.

Pattern: in each case the advantage is a mechanism (chokepoint control, a promise, a lease, externalizing a cost center), not just "being good".

Profit pools

U-Haul (late 1990s): earned a 10% operating margin when consumer truck rental earned under 3%. The money was in boxes, tape, insurance, hitches and storage, bought after the customer signed and stopped comparison shopping. U-Haul held truck rates down on purpose: the low-margin activity acquires the customer for the high-margin one.
Definition (Gadiesh and Gilbert, HBR 1998): total profit earned at every point along an industry's value chain. Profit concentration is often very different from revenue concentration.
Value chain = from your general ledger, shows your costs, efficiency instrument. Profit pool = from industry filings, shows everyone's profit, positioning instrument ("am I standing in the right part of the chain?").

The four steps

  1. Define boundaries. This step determines the answer, and no principle exists for drawing the line.
  2. Estimate total pool size (profit, not revenue).
  3. Estimate each activity's share. Hard; margins are rarely disclosed, so use pure-play comparables and triangulation.
  4. Check and reconcile. A quarter of the method is reconciliation: the authors knew the numbers would not tie out.

Drawing convention: x-axis = share of industry revenue, y-axis = operating margin, so block area = profit. Tall and narrow = small and rich. Wide and flat = large and poor.

STRAT 401 · Reading, without the reading

A pizza that cost five dollars, and what it teaches about strategy

A firm doesn't have costs. Activities do. This page walks through the whole reading: Porter's value chain, how to run the analysis, the Little Caesars case and what it hides, firms that win by owning one activity, and profit pools (where the money actually sits).

Garden City, Michigan. A pepperoni pizza sits in a warming rack. Nobody has ordered it yet. It was made to a forecast. When a customer walks in, the sale takes about 40 seconds. Price: $5, from 2004 until January 2022.

The obvious explanation is cheap ingredients, and it's wrong. The $5 pizza came from about a dozen activities, each built to cost less than the same activity at Domino's or Pizza Hut. One of them, the delivery driver, was removed entirely.

The one-sentence takeawayA value chain analysis breaks a firm into the things it actually does, so you can ask three questions of each one: What does it cost us? What drives that cost? Would a buyer notice if we did it differently?
Part 1 · The framework

What Porter actually proposed

Michael Porter, Competitive Advantage (1985). The usual view, then and now, is that competitive advantage belongs to firms: some are well run and some aren't. Porter's view went further than that: a firm is a collection of separate activities, and it wins or loses in each one on its own.

He grouped the activities into nine generic categories. Click any box to see what it is. Then turn on the Little Caesars overlay.

■ Support activities (4): run across all primary activities■ Primary (5): touch the product on its way to the buyer
Pick a box.
The wedge on the right is margin: what's left when the buyer's willingness to pay is higher than the combined cost of every activity to its left.

Adapted from Porter, Competitive Advantage (1985), Ch. 2 (the reading's Exhibit 1).

Part 2 · Two ideas people usually miss

These two matter more than the nine categories

Idea 1

The boxes are a starting point, not the answer

The nine are generic on purpose. The analysis only gets useful once you split an activity whose parts have different economics.

  • Airline "operations" covers gate turnaround and engine overhaul, which have almost nothing in common.
  • Little Caesars "marketing & sales" splits into national advertising (a fixed cost paid from a franchise fund) and the menu-board price, which isn't a cost at all. It's a promise.
TestIf every activity in your chain has the same cost driver, you haven't split them finely enough.
Idea 2

Advantage can sit between the boxes: linkages

A linkage exists when the cost or effectiveness of one activity depends on how another one is done. It's the least-used part of the framework.

Why linkages are hard to copy: a rival can see most single activities (store layouts, shelf prices, job postings, patents). What it can't easily see is which activity is subsidizing which.

Part 3 · Method

How to run a value chain analysis in five steps

The framework only describes. The analysis has to produce something you can act on. Each step goes wrong in a predictable way if you skip its questions. Click a step to open it.

Porter's 10 cost drivers: practice

Don't assume scale explains everything. Go through the drivers one at a time. Read the scenario and pick the driver that fits best.

Part 4 · Case

Little Caesars: a low cost position built one activity at a time

Its cost advantage isn't concentrated in one place. It's spread across the chain in small, deliberate decisions that reinforce each other.

The real savings come from what it doesn't do at allNo taking orders before making pizza. No drivers. At the Portal, no staffed counter. Removing an activity is the most reliable cost cut available, because the other option, doing the activity more cheaply than a rival, invites the rival to respond.

The linkage triangle: why "just sell a cheaper pizza" doesn't work

Each one only works because of the others:

  • Made-ahead production needs a narrow menu. Forecasting four products is manageable. Forecasting forty isn't.
  • A narrow menu needs a low price. Buyers demand variety when the price is high.
  • A low price needs high throughput per labor hour, which is exactly what made-ahead production delivers.

Pull out any one and the other two stop making sense. That's a chain in Porter's sense.

The price advantage has narrowed

2004: $5 Hot-N-Ready. One number: no coupon, no wait, no decision. It held for 18 years.
Jan 2022: rises to $5.55 (with 33% more pepperoni). No national price announced since.
Now: third-party menu trackers put it near $6.79. Meanwhile Domino's keeps running a "Best Deal Ever": any pizza, any toppings, $9.99.
July 2025: Little Caesars launches its first-ever value menu at $9.99, online only. Its CMO said the company sets trends rather than following them, but it was following. Online-only also moves the offer away from the walk-in, no-wait mechanic the whole cost chain was built to serve.
Still impressive, just a different storyLittle Caesars really did remove drivers, order-taking, counter labor, menu complexity and square footage. Net US units grew by 93 in 2025 while the category shrank (limited-service pizza −0.3%, Little Caesars +1.4%). But a large share of the savings was captured by the franchisor through the required supplier and the highest fee load in the category, not passed fully to operators or customers.
The lesson to rememberA value chain analysis tells you where the cost went out. It doesn't tell you who kept it. Ask both questions.
Part 6 · The opposite strategy

Own one link

Little Caesars does nearly the whole chain cheaply. The alternative is to take one activity and do it so far beyond everyone else that the rest of the industry has to come to you. Pick a firm.

Part 7 · Where the money sits

Profit pools

If activities have different economics, then somewhere along every chain there's a place where the money collects.

The U-Haul story (late 1990s)

U-Haul rented trucks for less than anyone else. It earned a 10% operating margin while the consumer truck-rental industry earned under 3%. But the trucks weren't where the money was.

The money was in boxes, tape, insurance, hitches and storage, which customers buy after signing the rental agreement, once they've stopped comparison shopping.

Operating margin. U-Haul kept rental rates low on purpose: the low-margin activity was how it acquired customers for the high-margin one.

Where the idea comes from

Orit Gadiesh & James Gilbert, two Harvard Business Review articles (1998). An industry's profit pool is the total profit earned at every point along its value chain. The key claim: where profit concentrates in an industry is often very different from where revenue concentrates.

A positioning tool: are we standing in the right part of the chain at all?

How to map one (Gadiesh & Gilbert's four steps)

1 Define the pool's boundaries. Where does the chain start and end? This step determines the answer, and no one has offered a principle for drawing the line.
2 Estimate the pool's total size. Total profit, not revenue, across every activity inside the boundary.
3 Estimate each activity's share. The hard step: activity-level margins are almost never disclosed. You rebuild them from comparable single-business companies and by triangulating.
4 Check and reconcile. The reading's dry point: a method that spends a quarter of its steps on reconciliation was written by people who knew the numbers wouldn't tie out.

The study's conclusion: farmer prices are disconnected from consumer prices, and value concentrates between the importer and the retailer.

The iPhone needs a warning labelThe commonly cited Kraemer, Linden & Dedrick study (Apple captures 58% of an iPhone 4's price as profit, versus about 2% for direct labor in China) uses 2010 data. It also isn't a full breakdown of the retail dollar, because carriers paid Apple at the time rather than buyers paying through retail.

How a profit pool is drawn: inside a car dealership (AutoNation 2025)

The convention: x-axis = share of revenue, y-axis = margin, so the area of each block = profit. A tall, narrow block is a small, rich activity. A wide, flat one is a large, poor one. Click a block.

AutoNation sold $27.6B of vehicles, parts and service and earned $4.9B of gross profit.

AutoNation FY2025 results. New vehicles and parts & service are from the reading. F&I is derived (22.8% − 17.5%; 77.2% − 47.6%). "Used vehicles & other" is the remainder. Block heights are gross margin, computed as (GP share ÷ revenue share) × the company's 17.8% overall gross margin.

The headlineFinance & insurance plus parts & service, the two smallest revenue lines at 22.8% of sales, produced 77.2% of gross profit. New cars were nearly half the revenue (48.9%) but only 13.4% of gross profit.

Back to the warming rack

The $5 pizza was never about cheap cheese. It came from a chain with no drivers, no order-takers, no counter transaction, a required distributor, four products instead of forty, 1,400 square feet instead of 3,000, and a forecast instead of an order ticket. Each of those is an activity someone else performs and Little Caesars doesn't.

A chain also changes over time. The price is no longer $5. The value menu now matches a competitor's price instead of setting it. The franchisor kept much of the savings. The rival that once had the expensive chain rebuilt it around carryout. None of that showed up in the diagram. It showed up in the numbers underneath it.

The closing questionDraw your own chain, not the generic nine, split until each box has its own economics. Put a real cost and a real asset against each one. Then ask: if you could defend only one of these activities to the last dollar, which would it be, and is it the one you're funding?

Cheat sheet

Everything on one screen

Core idea

  • A firm has no costs. Activities do.
  • 9 generic activities: 5 primary (inbound, operations, outbound, marketing & sales, service) and 4 support (infrastructure, HR, technology development, procurement).
  • Margin = buyer's willingness to pay − total activity cost.

Two ideas people miss

  • Split until the parts have different economics.
  • Linkages: one activity's cost depends on another's. They're hard to copy because they can't be observed.
  • Amazon's regions: no single activity got cheaper.

5-step analysis

  • 1 Split up activities
  • 2 Cost + assets for each box
  • 3 Cost drivers (10 of them)
  • 4 Work the linkages, including suppliers and channels
  • 5 Own / buy / ride on someone else's brand

10 cost drivers

  • Scale · learning · capacity utilization · linkages · interrelationships across business units · vertical integration · timing of entry · discretionary policy choices · location · institutional factors

Little Caesars

  • Removing activities beats doing them cheaper.
  • Made-ahead ↔ narrow menu ↔ low price.
  • But: AUV ~69% of Domino's, 11% fees vs 9.5%, investment floor 4×, ACSI last.
  • Ask where the cost went out and who kept it.

Own one link

  • Inbound: ASML (only EUV maker, Zeiss stake)
  • Operations: TSMC (promise not to compete with customers), YKK (leased machines, brand on the customer's product)
  • Outbound: Amazon (cost center → sold as a product)
  • Service: Ritz-Carlton ($2,000 discretion per employee)

Profit pools

  • Gadiesh & Gilbert 1998: profit ≠ revenue concentration.
  • Value chain = efficiency. Profit pool = positioning.
  • Chart: x = revenue share, y = margin, area = profit.
  • 4 steps: boundaries, size, shares, reconcile.

Pool examples

  • U-Haul: cheap trucks, profitable boxes
  • Coffee: 21% to farming, 23% tax (Germany)
  • AutoNation: 22.8% of revenue → 77.2% of gross profit
  • Delta Amex = 141% of op. income; Apple 85% of profit; Booking > 2× Marriott
